analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to prove benefits justify costs before issuing major health, safety, and environmental rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 286-141 on February 28, 1995, but the Senate committee never acted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how agencies like the EPA, OSHA, and FDA justify major health, safety, and environmental rules. Before issuing any rule expected to cost $25 million a year or more, an agency would have to show that the rule's benefits are likely to justify its costs, consider cheaper alternatives including market-based approaches, and pass outside peer review for the biggest rules — and courts could throw out any action whose underlying risk analysis didn't comply. Supporters framed this as steering finite resources toward the biggest risks; its practical effect would have been to make expensive protective rules harder and slower to issue, with new openings for regulated industries to challenge them in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — chemical makers, polluters, manufacturers, and other companies facing costly EPA, OSHA, FDA, and Mine Safety rules — gain the most. Every major rule would come with a formal benefits-justify-costs certification, a published comparison of cheaper alternatives, and, for rules over $100 million, external peer review that must be answered in writing; companies could then sue, since courts would have to find an agency action unlawful if its risk document didn't substantially comply. Clean-up plans over $5 million would face the same process, slowing Superfund-style cleanups.

how_it_helps.text: No major health, safety, or environmental rule could be issued unless the agency certified that its incremental benefits are 'likely to justify, and be reasonably related to' its costs, and this standard would override the decision criteria of the underlying statutes where they conflict [S4].

For any rule expected to cost $100 million a year or more, the agency's risk and cost analysis would need independent external peer review, and peer reviewers with a stake in the outcome could not be excluded as long as they disclosed it [S4].

Courts would have to declare an agency action unlawful if a significant risk assessment or characterization document in the record did not substantially comply with the bill's requirements, giving regulated parties a concrete legal hook for challenges [S4].

Agencies would have to publish analyses of alternatives, effects on small businesses and employment, and comparisons of risks with familiar everyday risks, and publish the certifications with the final rule [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People exposed to pollution, workplace hazards, and unsafe products pay, in the form of slower and weaker protective rules: agencies would need months or years of extra analysis, certification, and peer review before acting, and statutes that deliberately ignore cost in favor of health protection would be overridden. Federal, state, and local agencies would also bear the cost of producing the new documents, and environmental clean-up decisions over $5 million would be slowed by the same process.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to pollution and hazards

drawbacks.text: The bill's certifications would supersede the decision criteria of statutes like the Clean Air Act and Superfund law where they conflict, replacing standards that deliberately prioritize health over cost with a benefits-must-justify-costs test [S4].

Any determination to approve or reject an environmental clean-up plan costing over $5 million would be treated as a major rule subject to the cost-benefit process, adding analysis and potential litigation to hazardous-waste cleanups [S4].

An honest supporter would concede the process adds time: risk guidelines, comparative-risk studies, agency plans, and peer reviews would all have to be completed before or alongside new rules, with some requirements not taking effect for 18 months after enactment [S4].

The bill's own findings argue that regulations have delivered dramatic improvements but have been more costly and less effective than necessary, and that prioritizing the greatest risks is the goal — a cost-effectiveness argument with real force even under an honest reading [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — spending safety and environmental dollars where they do the most good — is legitimate, and better risk analysis and public reporting of costs have real value. But the mechanism leans heavily toward whoever is regulated: benefits like avoided cancers or deaths decades in the future are hard to quantify against immediate, countable compliance costs, so the certification test would systematically favor rules that are cheap to comply with over rules that protect people most. Combined with mandatory court review of paperwork compliance, the bill's likely effect was fewer, slower, and more litigable protections — a trade weighted toward regulated industries rather than a balanced redesign.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin three days after it was introduced, but the Senate just referred it to its Governmental Affairs Committee, which never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 23, 1995, referred to three House committees, and moved to the House floor under a special rule within two days [S1].

On February 28, 1995, a Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add peer-review conflict-of-interest prohibitions failed 174-250, with 170 of 204 Democrats in favor and only 3 of 229 Republicans [S6].
The House passed the bill 286-141 on February 28, 1995: 226 of 229 Republicans voted yes while only 60 of 204 Democrats did [S6].
The Senate received the bill on March 2, 1995, and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs, where no further action was recorded before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S6].
The bill had a single cosponsor, a Republican [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing health, safety, and environmental rules stayed on their original statutory footing, so the agencies' protective mandates and the public's current protections were preserved. Regulated industries did not get the new cost-benefit hurdle or the added court challenges they had sought — but they also avoided nothing, since the bill simply died rather than becoming law in either direction.

for.name: Rep. Robert S. Walker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 23, 1995, and managed its floor consideration; it reached a final vote three days later.

for.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
for.what_they_did: His majority's leadership scheduled the bill for floor action within days of introduction as part of the new Congress's early regulatory-reform agenda.

against.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a section on peer review programs and prohibitions of conflicts of interest; the motion failed 174-250.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 2, 1995, and never reported it out or brought it to a vote; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. William Roth
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 226 of 229 Republicans voted yes while only 60 of 204 Democrats did, and the failed motion to recommit was nearly the mirror image, with 170 of 204 Democrats for it and 3 of 229 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill covers the EPA and applies its cost-benefit certification and judicial-review hooks to major air, water, waste, and carcinogen rules, plus clean-up plans over $5 million — giving regulated companies a way to delay or challenge rules that cost them money to comply with. Their savings would come at the cost of slower public-health protection.

industries.industry: Workplace-safety-regulated industries (OSHA and Mine Safety rules)
industries.note: OSHA and the Mine Safety and Health Administration are among the covered agencies, so their costliest worker-protection rules would need benefits-justify-costs certifications and, above $100 million, external peer review. The savings for employers would come out of protections for workers.

Treating clean-up plan decisions over $5 million as major rules could slow Superfund and hazardous-waste cleanups and shift what gets approved. Cleanup firms would face a slower, more contested project pipeline.

industries.industry: Risk assessment, cost-benefit consulting, and peer-review services
industries.note: The bill would create a standing pipeline of paid work: agency risk assessments under new principles, comparative-risk studies, National Peer Review Panels, and industry-funded rebuttal analyses. Its stance toward the public is mixed — the work exists either way, but the industry profits from the bill's process requirements regardless of whether rules get stronger or weaker.
